title: Typing Errors and unknown in catch
summary: Treat a caught error as something you must inspect before using.
nestedConcepts: Narrow caught errors before reading them

subtopics.title: unknown
subtopics.explanation: `unknown` means a value exists but its type has not been safely established. Unlike `any`, TypeScript will not let you use it freely. It is like a sealed package that you must inspect before opening. In a `catch` block, begin with `unknown` because code can throw strings, objects, or other unexpected values. For example, an API helper may throw a string, so a catch block cannot assume every value has a message. For example, a library may reject a promise with a string instead of an Error object.

subtopics.title: Narrow caught errors before reading them
subtopics.explanation: Use a type check before reading an error’s properties. `value instanceof Error` recognizes ordinary JavaScript `Error` objects. It is like checking a package label before following its instructions. Some libraries throw custom values, so decide how your application handles those cases instead of assuming every failure has a `.message` field. For example, use a type check before reading a property from an unknown caught value. For example, use a type guard before reading a message property.

subtopics.title: Convert
subtopics.explanation: Convert unexpected failures into a message your application can safely display. A fallback such as “Something went wrong” is clearer than showing `[object Object]`. This is like translating an unclear report into a useful status. Keep the original value for controlled diagnostics where possible, while handling formatting without crashing again. For example, a safe fallback message keeps an error screen readable when the thrown value is unusual. For example, show users a safe summary while recording controlled diagnostics for developers.

subtopics.title: Show users safe error messages
subtopics.explanation: Do not show stack traces, file paths, or raw server responses to ordinary users. They can expose implementation details or private data. Think of the stack trace as a repair log for the maintenance team, not a public sign. Give users a helpful next step and record detailed diagnostics in an access-controlled system. For example, keep a request identifier in diagnostics while omitting tokens and private payloads. For example, do not include tokens or private response bodies in the diagnostic context.

subtopics.title: Log
subtopics.explanation: Log enough context to investigate a failure, such as an operation name and a request identifier. Remove passwords, access tokens, and personal data first. A useful log is like a service ticket: it helps locate the fault without publishing a customer’s private information. Test both the user message and the diagnostic path. For example, test both an Error object and a non-Error value in the error handling path. For example, test error handling with both ordinary and unexpected thrown values.

foundations.overview: A value caught by JavaScript can be almost anything, not only an `Error`. TypeScript therefore lets you treat it as `unknown` and asks you to check it before reading its properties. Think of `unknown` as a sealed package: inspect the label before using what is inside. Convert failures into safe messages, and keep private diagnostic details out of user-facing screens.
foundations.whyItMatters: Caught values are not guaranteed to share one shape. Safe narrowing protects error handling itself from failing while preserving useful, private diagnostics.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A lost-and-found box may contain anything; identify the item before describing it.
commonUseCases: Show a safe message after a failed request.
Log enough context for developers to investigate a bug.
Handle a rejected promise from an unfamiliar library.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every caught value is an Error instance.
commonMisconceptions.reality: JavaScript can throw strings, objects, or other values, so inspect before using properties.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Showing the raw stack trace helps every user.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Stack traces can expose private details; provide a safe message and protected diagnostics.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Casting an unknown value to Error validates it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A type assertion changes TypeScript’s belief, not the actual runtime value.

keyTakeaways: `unknown` means a value exists but its type has not been safely established.
Use a type check before reading an error’s properties.

Do not show stack traces, file paths, or raw server responses to ordinary users.

codeLab.title: Handle an Unknown Error Safely
codeLab.instructions: Return a useful message whether JavaScript throws an Error object or a different value.
codeLab.expectedOutput: The type checker accepts safe values and reports mismatches at compile time.
hints: Keep external values typed as unknown until you check them.
Use a type feature that preserves the exact information you need.
